context.guidance: Protect each Tier A and Tier B Personal Data Element at field or column level before it is stored, with keys held outside the data store, so that a database dump or a restored backup does not reveal the values. Disk or volume encryption protects only the storage medium, so it lowers severity without clearing the Finding. Until DPDP §44(2) omits IT Act §43A, that section's reasonable-security duty applies alongside Rule 6(1)(a).

value.fix: Stop storing the card number in plaintext. The `cardNum` column is a Tier A Personal Data Element (a payment card PAN), and as written it ends up readable in any database dump or restored backup. The best fix is to not store the PAN at all. Send it straight from the client to a PCI-DSS compliant payment gateway or vault (for example Razorpay, Stripe or Juspay tokenization) and keep only what comes back: the gateway token, the last 4 digits, the card brand and the expiry month/year. Replace `cardNum` with something like `«SECRET» type: DataTypes.STRING, allowNull: false }` and `cardLast4: { type: DataTypes.STRING(4), validate: { is: /^\d{4}$/ } }`. If the business truly has to keep the PAN, encrypt it in the application before it reaches the database. Use AES-256-GCM with envelope encryption: get a data key from an external KMS or HSM (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault), and never keep keys in the database, the repo or the same host's `.env`. Store the PAN as a `DataTypes.STRING` or `BLOB` holding `iv || ciphertext || authTag || keyId`, encrypting in a `beforeCreate`/`beforeUpdate` hook or a custom setter and decrypting only on authorized code paths. If you need to look cards up, add a separate `cardNumHmac` column (HMAC-SHA256 with a separate KMS-held key). Also fix the type: a 16-digit number doesn't fit in `DataTypes.INTEGER` (32-bit), and a PAN shouldn't be numeric anyway because leading zeros and PANs of 12 to 19 digits get lost. Before tokenizing or encrypting, validate it as a 12 to 19 digit string with a Luhn check instead of the `min`/`max` integer range. Then write a migration that encrypts or tokenizes the existing rows and drops the plaintext column. Rotate keys, purge or re-encrypt old backups and replicas that still hold plaintext PANs, keep PANs out of logs, error messages and API responses (show a masked `**** **** **** 1234`), and restrict decrypt permission through KMS IAM policy. Disk or TDE encryption can stay as defense in depth, but it doesn't close this finding. This meets DPDP Rule 6(1)(a), IT Act §43A reasonable security practices and PCI-DSS Req. 3.4/3.5. I haven't run or tested any of this against your codebase.
